derivations.claim: Finite smooth cutoffs and partitions on the compact corner charts are obtained from [F7]: restrict ambient Euclidean bumps to each half-space or quadrant chart, using a strict support margin to extend by zero. Choose a finite family whose smaller chart neighborhoods cover the compact set, and divide its bumps by their positive sum there. Thus the interpolation below uses actual finite smooth partitions without applying a boundaryless manifold theorem to corners. A corner in a compact surface with faces is isolated, so compactness gives finitely many corners. Choose pairwise disjoint quadrant charts about them; their two coordinate directions give product collars of the incident faces that agree on the quadrant. Delete smaller quadrant neighborhoods and round the new boundary junctions inside those neighborhoods. The remaining ambient surface is a smooth manifold with boundary, so [F4] gives collars of its remaining original boundary arcs. Restrict those collars to the black and free arcs. On each overlap with a corner chart, interpolate their inward transverse vector fields with the coordinate normal field by a smooth partition of unity, taking the coordinate field on a smaller corner neighborhood. Positive inward normal components remain positive under this interpolation. Near a corner use the two coordinate fields for the two incident faces; they commute there and are tangent to the other face. Their smooth ambient local flows from [F8], restricted to inward times and a common sufficiently small width on each compact face, give face collars equal to the fixed product collars in the smaller quadrant. Away from corners the two faces do not meet, so no further compatibility is required. This finite construction gives the compatible face collars in the definition. A black face glues to an oppositely oriented black face of the same type, and the interval endpoint colors match by the stated rule; therefore the quotient retains an oriented surface with corners and the unglued free faces retain their labels.

Replacing either collar by a shorter collar or a smooth increasing reparameterization of its normal coordinate changes the glued surface by a diffeomorphism that is the identity outside the seam collars and on the residual black boundary. A boundary-relative diffeomorphism of either input extends over its product collar by the product map and hence descends to the glued quotient. Thus gluing is independent of representatives and collar widths in the stated equivalence class.

For three composable representatives, both parenthesized composites identify the same three collared surfaces along the same two black boundary parameterizations. In product coordinates, both quotients are obtained by replacing the two seam collars by the same concatenated interval; a smooth increasing reparameterization of that interval gives a diffeomorphism fixed on the exterior black boundary. Hence composition is associative on equivalence classes. Gluing an identity cylinder merely lengthens a collar and is equivalent to the original surface by step 2.1.

Ordered disjoint union is associative with the empty surface as strict unit at the level of words and diffeomorphism classes. The cylinder that permutes components gives the symmetry; composition of these cylinders is permutation composition, and its double application is the identity permutation. The interchange law holds because gluing and disjoint union act on disjoint collared components. Thus the category is strict symmetric monoidal, and [F2]–[F3] identify its required coherence data.

The condition $\partial_1M=\varnothing$ is preserved by gluing and disjoint union, so the circle-only objects and no-free-boundary morphisms form the stated closed symmetric monoidal subcategory. The excluded full-subcategory convention would admit a morphism with a nonempty free circular face, which violates $\partial_1M=\varnothing$.

For the strong monoidal functors of [F5], identity natural transformations satisfy the binary and unit compatibility equations of [F6]; if two transformations satisfy them, substitution in those equations shows their componentwise vertical composite also satisfies them. Their identity and associativity laws hold componentwise in the target category [F1]. Thus the morphisms between the functors in the definition form the stated category.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

A **monoidal category** is a category $\mathcal C$ equipped with:

- a bifunctor $\otimes:\mathcal C\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$
  ([[def-product-category]], [[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]);
- an object $\mathbf 1$ of $\mathcal C$;
- natural isomorphisms ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])
  $$\alpha_{X,Y,Z}:((X\otimes Y)\otimes Z)\longrightarrow X\otimes(Y\otimes Z),$$
  $$\lambda_X:(\mathbf 1\otimes X)\longrightarrow X,\qquad \rho_X:(X\otimes\mathbf 1)\longrightarrow X,$$

such that the following two equations hold for all objects
$W,X,Y,Z\in\mathcal C$.

The **pentagon axiom** is

$$\alpha_{W,X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{W\otimes X,Y,Z}=(1_W\otimes\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ\alpha_{W,X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(\alpha_{W,X,Y}\otimes1_Z).$$

The **triangle axiom** is

$$(1_X\otimes\lambda_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,\mathbf 1,Y}=\rho_X\otimes1_Y.$$

This page imposes no further axiom. In particular, the equality
$\lambda_{\mathbf 1}=\rho_{\mathbf 1}$ is not built into the definition; it is
derived later on this page.

A **symmetric monoidal category** is a braided monoidal category
([[def-braided-monoidal-category]]) whose braiding $c$ satisfies

$$c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}=1_{X\otimes Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Let
$(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ and
$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

A strong monoidal functor is **strict monoidal** when the functor preserves the
unit and tensor on the nose and every structure map above is an identity.

Let $F,G:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ be lax monoidal functors
([[def-lax-strong-and-strict-monoidal-functor]]).
A **monoidal natural transformation** $\theta:F\Rightarrow G$ is a natural
transformation ([[def-natural-transformation]]) such that

$$\theta_{X\otimes Y}\circ F_{2;X,Y}=G_{2;X,Y}\circ(\theta_X\boxtimes\theta_Y)$$

for all objects $X,Y$, and

$$G_0=\theta_{\mathbf 1}\circ F_0.$$

Thus $\theta$ is compatible both with the binary structure maps and with the
unit map.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

derivations.claim: Choose a basis $(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$ of $A$. The map $\Theta:A\to A^*$ given by $\Theta(v)(a)=\epsilon(av)$ is an isomorphism by [F1]. Define $v_i:=\Theta^{-1}(u_i^*)$. Then $\epsilon(u_jv_i)=\delta_{ji}$, and [F2] gives $a=\sum_i\epsilon(av_i)u_i,\qquad a=\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i a).$ For the second identity, apply $z\mapsto\epsilon(u_jz)$ to its proposed right side: $\sum_i\epsilon(u_jv_i)\epsilon(u_i a)=\epsilon(u_j a)$. These functionals separate elements by nondegeneracy in the second variable, so the right side equals $a$. Set $e:=\sum_i v_i\otimes u_i$.

Conversely, suppose $(A,\mu,\eta,\Delta,\epsilon)$ satisfies [F3], and put $d:=\Delta\circ\eta:k\to A\otimes A$. With the canonical associators and unitors, the two snake composites are $S_L:=\rho_A\circ(1_A\otimes\beta)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(d\otimes1_A)\circ\lambda_A^{-1}:A\to A$ and $S_R:=\lambda_A\circ(\beta\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes d)\circ\rho_A^{-1}:A\to A.$ For $S_L$, replace $\beta$ by $\epsilon\mu$ and use the Frobenius identity $(1_A\otimes\mu)\alpha(\Delta\otimes1_A)=\Delta\mu$; naturality of $\alpha$ moves $\eta$ to the first input. The left unit equation reduces the composite to $\rho_A(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\Delta$, which is $1_A$ by the right counit. For $S_R$, use $(\mu\otimes1_A)\alpha^{-1}(1_A\otimes\Delta)=\Delta\mu$; the right unit equation reduces it to $\lambda_A(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\Delta$, which is $1_A$ by the left counit. Thus both snake composites are identities.

The first displayed dual-basis identity gives $\sum_i\epsilon(a v_i)u_i=a$, and the second gives $\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i a)=a$, so this $e$ has the required two contraction properties. If another tensor has the first property, contracting its first factor against every functional $x\mapsto\epsilon(a x)$ gives the same vector for every fixed $a$; these functionals range over all of $A^*$ by nondegeneracy. Hence the tensors are equal. The contraction map $A\otimes A\to\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^*,A)$ is an isomorphism in finite dimension, so the tensor is intrinsically defined and independent of the basis.

To prove $(a\otimes1)e=e(1\otimes a)$, test the two tensors against arbitrary $\phi\otimes\psi\in A^*\otimes A^*$. Nondegeneracy supplies $c,d\in A$ with $\phi(z)=\epsilon(cz)$ and $\psi(z)=\epsilon(zd)$. The first contraction is $\sum_i\epsilon(cav_i)\epsilon(u_i d)=\epsilon(cad)$ by the second dual-basis identity applied to $d$. The second is $\sum_i\epsilon(cv_i)\epsilon(u_iad)=\epsilon(cad)$ by the same identity applied to $ad$. Since such product functionals separate tensors, the two tensors agree.

Define $\Delta(a)=(a\otimes1)e$. Then $(\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta(a)=\sum_i\epsilon(av_i)u_i=a$. Also $(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta(a)=a\sum_i v_i\epsilon(u_i)=a$ by the second identity in step 1.1 at $a=1$. The central relation of step 2.2 gives $\Delta(ab)=(a\otimes1)\Delta(b)=\Delta(a)(1\otimes b).$ Expanding these two equalities with the associator is exactly the pair of Frobenius identities in [F3].

The defining contraction also yields, for all $x,y,a\in A$, $(\beta\otimes\beta)(x\otimes y,\Delta(a)) =\sum_i\epsilon(xav_i)\epsilon(yu_i) =\epsilon(yxa)=\beta(yx,a).$ This establishes the contraction identity.

If $\Delta'$ is another coproduct with counit $\epsilon$ and the two Frobenius identities, write $e'=\Delta'(1)=\sum_jx'_j\otimes y'_j$. Applying the counit identities to $\Delta'(a)$ and using each Frobenius identity gives $\sum_j\epsilon(ax'_j)y'_j=a,\qquad \sum_jx'_j\epsilon(y'_j a)=a.$ Step 2.1 therefore gives $e'=e$. The Frobenius identity then gives $\Delta'(a)=(a\otimes1)e'=(a\otimes1)e=\Delta(a)$, so the coproduct is unique.

Use the tensor-product pairing $\beta^{\otimes3}$ to test coassociativity. For any $x,y,z,a\in A$, step 4.1 gives $\langle x\otimes y\otimes z,(\Delta\otimes1)\Delta(a)\rangle =\beta(zyx,a) =\langle x\otimes y\otimes z,(1\otimes\Delta)\Delta(a)\rangle.$ The pairing $\beta^{\otimes3}$ is nondegenerate: in any basis its matrix is the Kronecker product of three invertible matrices for $\beta$. Thus the two tensors are equal, proving coassociativity.

The two snake identities exhibit inverse maps between $A$ and $A^*$ for the left and right pairings, respectively; hence $\beta$ is nondegenerate in both variables. It follows that $\epsilon$ is a Frobenius functional by [F1], and step 4.2 gives uniqueness of $\Delta$. Symmetry of $\beta$ and commutativity of $\mu$ remain the separate properties defined in [F3].

Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). A bilinear form $\beta:A\times A\to k$ is **associative** when $\beta(ab,c)=\beta(a,bc)$ for all $a,b,c\in A$. It is **nondegenerate** when both linear maps
$$
A\to A^*,\qquad a\mapsto[b\mapsto\beta(a,b)],\qquad b\mapsto[a\mapsto\beta(a,b)]
$$
are isomorphisms. A linear functional $\lambda:A\to k$ is a **Frobenius functional** when $\beta_\lambda(a,b):=\lambda(ab)$ is nondegenerate. Associativity of $\beta_\lambda$ follows from associativity of multiplication. The algebra $A$ is **Frobenius** when it has at least one Frobenius functional.
If $B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)$ is a basis of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, then its dual family $B^*=(b_1^*,\ldots,b_n^*)$ is a basis of $V^*$. Consequently $\dim V^*=\dim V=n$.

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad \Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu =(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A) =(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
\mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
$$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
\eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
$$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}} =\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}}, \qquad \mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1}, \qquad (1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd} =(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba} =\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad \eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}}) =\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*) =\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^* =\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad \Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad \epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad \Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

derivations.claim: If $M=\varnothing$, use the empty function and empty generator word; all assertions are vacuous. For nonempty $M$, the finite bump and partition constructions used below also work in its corner charts: extend a chart to an ambient Euclidean open set, use [F8] on nested balls there, restrict to the half-space or quadrant, and extend by zero outside the chart. A strict support margin makes that extension smooth, including on boundary faces. Smaller restricted balls cover each compact set in question; choose a finite subcover. The corresponding nonnegative bumps $b_j$ have positive sum near that compact set, so $b_j/\sum_i b_i$ form a smooth finite subordinate partition there. Each selected bump is one on a smaller chart neighborhood. For a cutoff equal to one near an entire compact set and supported in a prescribed open neighborhood use $1-\prod_j(1-b_j)$; its support lies in the finite union of the strict chart supports. This proves the corner-chart partition and cutoff assertions directly from [F8], rather than applying a boundaryless partition theorem to corners. There are finitely many corners: the depth-two stratum of a compact surface with faces is a closed discrete zero-manifold, so its singleton neighborhoods have a finite subcover. Choose disjoint quadrant charts at these corners. The two coordinate directions in each quadrant give product collars of the two incident faces. Delete smaller quadrant neighborhoods, round their new junctions inside those neighborhoods, and apply [F2] to the remaining ambient smooth surface with boundary. Restrict its collars to the remaining original face arcs. Interpolate the associated inward transverse fields with the coordinate normal fields on the finite overlaps, keeping the latter fields fixed in smaller quadrant charts. Positivity of the inward component is preserved by the partition-of-unity interpolation. Fix a set $S$ of **boundary colors**. A **black boundary component** is a parametrized incoming or outgoing boundary circle or interval. A **free boundary component** is a connected component of the remaining boundary, labeled by one element of $S$. The intersection of a black and a free face consists of **corners**. A smooth structure with corners means that every point has a chart in an open subset of $[0,\infty)^r\times\mathbb R^{2-r}$, $0\le r\le2$, and transition maps extend smoothly to open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$.

Each surface representative is equipped with smooth collars of its black and free faces that are product collars in the quadrant charts at corners. A collar of a face $F$ is a smooth embedding $F\times[0,\epsilon)\to M$ restricting to the identity on $F\times\{0\}$. The collars are used only to define gluing; morphisms forget their lengths and are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that fix every black parameterization, preserve incoming/outgoing faces, and preserve each free-boundary color. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, compatible collars exist: use the smooth collar theorem on rounded ambient surface pieces and the finite chart-and-flow construction below to retain the prescribed product collars at corners.

An **object** is a finite ordered word in:

- the positively oriented circle $C$; and
- intervals $I_{ab}$, for $a,b\in S$, oriented from their left endpoint of color $a$ to their right endpoint of color $b$.

The empty word is allowed. A **morphism** from a word $X$ to a word $Y$ is an equivalence class of compact oriented smooth surfaces with corners whose black boundary is the disjoint union of a parameterized incoming copy of $X$ and a parameterized outgoing copy of $Y$, with the induced boundary orientations opposite to the object orientations on incoming components and equal on outgoing components. Every free-boundary component is colored in $S$. No free boundary is required to be connected, and a free component may be a circle (a window) or an interval between corners.

Composition glues the outgoing black boundary of the first surface to the incoming black boundary of the second, component by component, using the fixed parameterizations. A circle matches a circle; $I_{ab}$ matches the oppositely oriented copy of that same interval, with its endpoint colors in the reversed boundary orientation. Tensor product is ordered disjoint union and concatenation of words. The symmetry is the cylinder with the ordered boundary components permuted. The identity on a word is its product cylinder.

Write $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ for this symmetric monoidal category. Its objects include circle and interval words and its morphisms may have colored free boundary.

The **closed oriented surface category** $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2$ has only finite words of circles as objects and only morphisms with no free boundary at all. It is not the full subcategory of $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ on circle words: that full subcategory would also contain circle-to-circle surfaces with free-boundary windows.

For a field $k$, $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is the category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps with the usual tensor product, unit $k$, associator, unitors, and flip. A (closed or open-closed) **2D TQFT** here is a strong symmetric monoidal functor from the indicated surface category to $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$. Morphisms of TQFTs are monoidal natural transformations, with the binary and unit compatibility equations of [[def-monoidal-natural-transformation]].
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a positive-dimensional smooth manifold, let $\mathcal A$ be a smooth
atlas on $M$, and let $E\subseteq M$ be $\mathcal A$-null in the sense of
[[def-null-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold]]. Then $M\setminus E$ is dense in $M$.
In particular, under Countable Choice the conclusion holds for any manifold-null
set $E$.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth.

- The function $f$ is a **Morse function** when every critical point of $f$ is
  nondegenerate
  ([[def-critical-point-and-critical-value-of-a-smooth-function]],
  [[def-nondegenerate-critical-point-nullity-index-and-coindex]]).
- The function $f$ is an **excellent Morse function** when it is Morse and any
  two distinct critical points have distinct critical values.

Thus excellence is stronger than the Morse condition: it excludes repeated
critical values, not repeated indices.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. For each $p\in M$, let
$\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ be the maximal integral curve through $p$, and set

$$ \mathcal D:=\{(t,p)\in\mathbb R\times M:t\in I_p\}, \qquad \Phi(t,p):=\gamma_p(t). $$

Then $\mathcal D$ is open in $\mathbb R\times M$, each fibre $\mathcal D_p$ is
an interval containing $0$, the map $\Phi:\mathcal D\to M$ is smooth, and
$\Phi$ is the unique maximal local flow generated by $X$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with boundary and let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ tangent to $\partial M$. Then $X$ has a local two-sided ambient flow, and every defined time slice preserves $\partial M$.

derivations.claim: We first give the elementary cut procedure used in every certificate below. Let $P(B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_h)$ be a round disk with $h$ disjoint smaller round disks removed. Each $B_j$ is the cyclic word of marked black intervals and colored free arcs on that component, or a single marked black circle. The orientation on $B_0$ is opposite to that on the interior holes, as dictated by the surface orientation. A word is always read in the induced surface-boundary direction; $X^-$ and $U^+$ denote an incoming and outgoing black slot. To cut $P$ into a disk, pick a nonblack basepoint on each component with such a point, or a basepoint on a black circle otherwise, and draw disjoint arcs $s_j$ from $B_0$ to $B_j$. Arrange the arcs at the root in the order $1,\ldots,h$. After cutting them the disk boundary word is $B_0s_1B_1s_1^{-1}s_2B_2s_2^{-1}\cdots s_hB_hs_h^{-1}.$ Black circle basepoints are auxiliary, not extra markings. A desired circle parameterization is respected on its whole collar, including this point. If two cut patches have this same word, match the corresponding black collars by their parameterizations and match each colored free arc by an increasing smooth map. Match the two sides of every $s_j$ by identical product maps. This gives a disk-boundary map extending to the collars. After rounding the nonblack corners, lift the remaining angular map $h$ to a strictly increasing map of $\mathbb R$ with $h(\theta+2\pi)=h(\theta)+2\pi$. The interpolation $(1-u)\theta+uh(\theta)$ has positive derivative for $0\le u\le1$. Use $u=0$ near the center and $u=1$ near the boundary; its polar extension is smooth and orientation preserving, and agrees with the prescribed collar map after the collar is attached. Regluing the paired $s_j$ edges gives the desired diffeomorphism. This proves the cut criterion directly for these planar models; no surface normal-form theorem is used.

Here are the three gluing rules for computing the certificates. A disk generator with cyclic word $EX$ glued to another disk with word $X^{-1}D$ along an interval seam $X$ becomes the disk with word $ED$; this follows by placing the two collars along the two sides of the same straight segment in a disk. If either disk has holes, carry their disjoint removed disks through this construction; the holes are simply retained. Gluing a boundary circle of one planar patch to one of a different planar patch joins their annular collars and gives a planar patch with the unglued boundary components; this can be seen by placing one punctured disk in the deleted disk of the other, using inversion of the annular radial coordinate on the collar. Finally, two disks glued along two disjoint interval seams give an annulus when the boundary splicing yields two boundary cycles. To check this without a classification theorem, first glue one seam to obtain a disk; the second seam identifies two boundary intervals with opposite induced orientations. Their standard rectangular collar is a strip joining those intervals outside the disk. The two complementary boundary arcs are distinct, and a cut through that strip returns a disk. Its regluing is precisely $P(B_0;B_1)$. All these constructions respect the marked portions of the boundary. The rule for one interval seam can be applied repeatedly to any tree of disk/annulus patches.

A product generator is a disk with cyclic boundary word $U_{ac}^{+}F_cY_{bc}^{-}F_bX_{ab}^{-}F_a$. A coproduct generator is the same disk read with reversed heights, with word $U_{ab}^{+}F_bV_{bc}^{+}F_cX_{ac}^{-}F_a$. The unit and counit are disks with a single black interval and its complementary free arc. A zipper is an annulus with words $(U_{aa}^{+}F_a;X_C^{-})$, and a cozipper is an annulus with words $(X_{aa}^{-}F_a;U_C^{+})$. The closed product and coproduct are punctured disks with three marked circle boundaries; the closed unit and counit have one. These are concrete choices of the elementary patches. The gluing rules in step 2.1 give the following exhaustive table for the defining equations of the data definition. In the table each displayed word belongs to an individual full boundary component; a semicolon separates components. $F_a$ means one free arc of color $a$, including the case of the complementary arc of a single marked interval.

Every row is a finite application of the gluing rules to specified disks or punctured disks. The rules prove planarity by construction; planarity is not inferred merely from an Euler characteristic or an appeal to the classification under proof. For an open row with one boundary component the displayed word is already the cut disk. For the other rows cut the indicated root-to-hole arcs, and use step 1.1. The identical words and paired seam sides give orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms fixed on every external black collar and preserving each free-edge label. In particular the Cardy row retains separate $a$- and $b$-labeled boundary components, and the open Frobenius rows retain their different domains and codomains. The cyclic trace row allows rotation of the disk boundary word but fixes the actual black slots after their specified symmetry; it gives no open commutativity assertion.

The rows give the closed Frobenius, open indexed Frobenius, cyclic trace, zipper algebra, centrality, pairing adjunction and Cardy equations of the data definition. A strong symmetric monoidal functor preserves composition, tensor, identities and the symmetry cylinders, and carries the product-cylinder associators and unitors to its tensor comparison maps coherently. Applying it to these actual surface equalities therefore gives exactly the typed equations in the data definition. No relation-completeness assertion has been used.

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad \Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu =(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A) =(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
\mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
$$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
\eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
$$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}} =\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}}, \qquad \mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1}, \qquad (1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd} =(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba} =\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad \eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}}) =\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*) =\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^* =\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad \Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad \epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad \Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

Let
$(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ and
$(\mathcal D,\boxtimes,\mathbf 1',\alpha',\lambda',\rho')$
be monoidal categories ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **lax monoidal functor** is a functor
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]])
together with natural transformations ([[def-natural-transformation]])

$$F_{2;X,Y}:F(X)\boxtimes F(Y)\longrightarrow F(X\otimes Y),$$

and

the morphism

$$F_0:\mathbf 1'\longrightarrow F(\mathbf 1),$$

such that, for all $X,Y,Z$,

$$F(\alpha_{X,Y,Z})\circ F_{2;X\otimes Y,Z}\circ(F_{2;X,Y}\boxtimes1_{F(Z)})=F_{2;X,Y\otimes Z}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_{2;Y,Z})\circ\alpha'_{F(X),F(Y),F(Z)},$$

$$F(\lambda_X)\circ F_{2;\mathbf 1,X}\circ(F_0\boxtimes1_{F(X)})=\lambda'_{F(X)},$$

$$F(\rho_X)\circ F_{2;X,\mathbf 1}\circ(1_{F(X)}\boxtimes F_0)=\rho'_{F(X)}.$$

A lax monoidal functor is **strong monoidal** when the natural transformation
$F_2$ is a natural isomorphism ([[def-natural-isomorphism]])—equivalently,
every component $F_{2;X,Y}$ is an isomorphism—and $F_0$ is an isomorphism.

A strong monoidal functor is **strict monoidal** when the functor preserves the
unit and tensor on the nose and every structure map above is an identity.

A **symmetric monoidal category** is a braided monoidal category
([[def-braided-monoidal-category]]) whose braiding $c$ satisfies

$$c_{Y,X}\circ c_{X,Y}=1_{X\otimes Y}$$

for all objects $X,Y$.

Fix a set $S$ of **boundary colors**. A **black boundary component** is a parametrized incoming or outgoing boundary circle or interval. A **free boundary component** is a connected component of the remaining boundary, labeled by one element of $S$. The intersection of a black and a free face consists of **corners**. A smooth structure with corners means that every point has a chart in an open subset of $[0,\infty)^r\times\mathbb R^{2-r}$, $0\le r\le2$, and transition maps extend smoothly to open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$.

Each surface representative is equipped with smooth collars of its black and free faces that are product collars in the quadrant charts at corners. A collar of a face $F$ is a smooth embedding $F\times[0,\epsilon)\to M$ restricting to the identity on $F\times\{0\}$. The collars are used only to define gluing; morphisms forget their lengths and are identified by orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms that fix every black parameterization, preserve incoming/outgoing faces, and preserve each free-boundary color. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, compatible collars exist: use the smooth collar theorem on rounded ambient surface pieces and the finite chart-and-flow construction below to retain the prescribed product collars at corners.

An **object** is a finite ordered word in:

- the positively oriented circle $C$; and
- intervals $I_{ab}$, for $a,b\in S$, oriented from their left endpoint of color $a$ to their right endpoint of color $b$.

The empty word is allowed. A **morphism** from a word $X$ to a word $Y$ is an equivalence class of compact oriented smooth surfaces with corners whose black boundary is the disjoint union of a parameterized incoming copy of $X$ and a parameterized outgoing copy of $Y$, with the induced boundary orientations opposite to the object orientations on incoming components and equal on outgoing components. Every free-boundary component is colored in $S$. No free boundary is required to be connected, and a free component may be a circle (a window) or an interval between corners.

Composition glues the outgoing black boundary of the first surface to the incoming black boundary of the second, component by component, using the fixed parameterizations. A circle matches a circle; $I_{ab}$ matches the oppositely oriented copy of that same interval, with its endpoint colors in the reversed boundary orientation. Tensor product is ordered disjoint union and concatenation of words. The symmetry is the cylinder with the ordered boundary components permuted. The identity on a word is its product cylinder.

Write $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ for this symmetric monoidal category. Its objects include circle and interval words and its morphisms may have colored free boundary.

The **closed oriented surface category** $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{cl}}_2$ has only finite words of circles as objects and only morphisms with no free boundary at all. It is not the full subcategory of $\mathsf{Cob}^{\mathrm{oc}}_2(S)$ on circle words: that full subcategory would also contain circle-to-circle surfaces with free-boundary windows.

For a field $k$, $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is the category of finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps with the usual tensor product, unit $k$, associator, unitors, and flip. A (closed or open-closed) **2D TQFT** here is a strong symmetric monoidal functor from the indicated surface category to $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$. Morphisms of TQFTs are monoidal natural transformations, with the binary and unit compatibility equations of [[def-monoidal-natural-transformation]].

Fix a field $k$ and write $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ for finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces and linear maps, with the algebraic tensor product, unit object $k$, canonical associator $\alpha_{U,V,W}: (U\otimes V)\otimes W\to U\otimes(V\otimes W)$, unitors $\lambda_U:k\otimes U\to U$ and $\rho_U:U\otimes k\to U$, and flip $\tau_{U,V}:U\otimes V\to V\otimes U$. The associator sends $(u\otimes v)\otimes w$ to $u\otimes(v\otimes w)$; the unitors send $c\otimes u$ and $u\otimes c$ to $cu$. All tensor expressions below use these maps, so no strictification is implicit.

A **Frobenius object** in $\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathrm{fd}}(k)$ is a finite-dimensional vector space $A$ and linear maps
$$
\mu:A\otimes A\to A,\qquad \eta:k\to A,\qquad \Delta:A\to A\otimes A,\qquad \epsilon:A\to k
$$
such that $(A,\mu,\eta)$ is a unital associative algebra, $(A,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a counital coassociative coalgebra, and the two Frobenius identities hold:
$$
\Delta\circ\mu =(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A) =(\mu\otimes1_A)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A,A,A}\circ(1_A\otimes\Delta).
$$
Here associativity is $\mu\circ(\mu\otimes1_A)=\mu\circ(1_A\otimes\mu)\circ\alpha_{A,A,A}$, and the two unit equations use $\lambda_A,\rho_A$. Coassociativity is $\alpha_{A,A,A}\circ(\Delta\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=(1_A\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$, and the counit equations are $(\epsilon\otimes1_A)\circ\Delta=\lambda_A^{-1}$ and $(1_A\otimes\epsilon)\circ\Delta=\rho_A^{-1}$.

Its **Frobenius pairing** is $b_A:=\epsilon\circ\mu:A\otimes A\to k$. It is **symmetric** when $b_A=b_A\circ\tau_{A,A}$. It is **commutative** when $\mu=\mu\circ\tau_{A,A}$. These are different conditions: commutativity implies symmetry of $b_A$, but symmetry of $b_A$ does not assert commutativity of $\mu$.

An **S-colored knowledgeable Frobenius datum** consists of:

- a commutative Frobenius object $(C,\mu_C,\eta_C,\Delta_C,\epsilon_C)$;
- a finite-dimensional vector space $A_{ab}$ for every ordered pair $a,b\in S$;
- maps, for every $a,b,c\in S$,
  $$
\mu_{abc}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}\to A_{ac},\quad \Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc},
$$
  and, for every $a\in S$,
  $$
\eta_a:k\to A_{aa},\quad \epsilon_a:A_{aa}\to k,\quad i_a:C\to A_{aa},\quad i_a^*:A_{aa}\to C.
$$

These maps obey the following typed equations. The first eight equations are the colored category, unit, coalgebra, counit, and Frobenius laws. The two Frobenius equalities are written separately by their domains and codomains; this avoids chaining opposite-direction composites into one equation.

1. For $a,b,c,d\in S$, associativity is
$$
\mu_{abd}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}} =\mu_{acd}\circ(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $(A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc})\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ad}$.

2. The left and right units are
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(\eta_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})=\lambda_{A_{ab}}, \qquad \mu_{abb}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\eta_b)=\rho_{A_{ab}}.
$$

3. Coassociativity and the two counits are
$$
\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\Delta_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd})\circ\Delta_{abd},
$$
$$
(\epsilon_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}})\circ\Delta_{aab}=\lambda_{A_{ab}}^{-1}, \qquad (1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\epsilon_b)\circ\Delta_{abb}=\rho_{A_{ab}}^{-1}.
$$

4. The two typed Frobenius identities are
$$
\Delta_{abd}\circ\mu_{acd} =(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\mu_{bcd})\circ\alpha_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}}),
$$
as maps $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}$, and
$$
\Delta_{acd}\circ\mu_{abd} =(\mu_{abc}\otimes1_{A_{cd}})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{A_{ab},A_{bc},A_{cd}}\circ(1_{A_{ab}}\otimes\Delta_{bcd}),
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{bd}\to A_{ac}\otimes A_{cd}$.

5. The trace is cyclic across opposite colors:
$$
\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba} =\epsilon_b\circ\mu_{bab}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}
$$
as maps $A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k$.

6. Each $i_a$ is a unital algebra map, its image acts centrally on each $A_{ab}$, and $i_a^*$ is pairing-adjoint to $i_a$:
$$
\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes i_a)=i_a\circ\mu_C,\qquad \eta_a=i_a\circ\eta_C,
$$
$$
\mu_{aab}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{ab}}) =\mu_{abb}\circ\tau_{A_{bb},A_{ab}}\circ(i_b\otimes1_{A_{ab}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}$, and
$$
\epsilon_C\circ\mu_C\circ(1_C\otimes i_a^*) =\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aaa}\circ(i_a\otimes1_{A_{aa}})
$$
as maps $C\otimes A_{aa}\to k$.

7. The colored Cardy equation is
$$
i_a\circ i_b^* =\mu_{aba}\circ\tau_{A_{ba},A_{ab}}\circ\Delta_{bab}:A_{bb}\to A_{aa}.
$$
In particular, the reverse labels on $A_{ba}$ and $A_{ab}$ are required for the displayed composites to type-check.

A **homomorphism** from unprimed to primed S-colored data is a family of linear maps $f_C:C\to C'$ and $f_{ab}:A_{ab}\to A'_{ab}$ such that $f_C$ preserves the four Frobenius maps on $C$:
$$
\mu'_C(f_C\otimes f_C)=f_C\mu_C,\quad f_C\eta_C=\eta'_C,\quad \Delta'_C f_C=(f_C\otimes f_C)\Delta_C,\quad \epsilon'_C f_C=\epsilon_C,
$$
and
$$
\mu'_{abc}(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})=f_{ac}\mu_{abc},\quad f_{aa}\eta_a=\eta'_a,\quad \Delta'_{abc}f_{ac}=(f_{ab}\otimes f_{bc})\Delta_{abc},
$$
$$
\epsilon'_a f_{aa}=\epsilon_a,\quad f_{aa}i_a=i'_a f_C,\quad f_C i_a^*=i_a^{*'}f_{aa}
$$
for all indicated labels. Composition and identities are componentwise. For singleton $S=\{*\}$, write $A=A_{**}$, $i=i_*$, and $i^*=i_*^*$; this is the usual pair $(A,C,i,i^*)$.

For each $a,b\in S$, define the open pairing
$$
b_{ab}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k,\qquad b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\circ\mu_{aba}.
$$
The cyclic trace equation above identifies $b_{ab}$ with the reversed pairing $b_{ba}\circ\tau_{A_{ab},A_{ba}}$. The equations do not impose nondegeneracy as a separate axiom: [[lem-frobenius-sewing-derived-moves]] proves that both induced maps to algebraic duals are isomorphisms, by exhibiting the two snake composites. For $a=b$, this is the symmetric Frobenius pairing on $A_{aa}$.

No equality $C=Z(A_{aa})$ is part of the definition. The Cardy equation is an additional map equality; it does not identify the underlying vector spaces or force the whole open algebra to be commutative.

For S-colored knowledgeable data of [[def-frobenius-object-and-knowledgeable-sewing-data]], all of the following identities follow from its typed equations: open and closed evaluation/coevaluation snakes; symmetry and cyclic invariance of the pairings and their adjoint copairings; both zipper/cozipper pairing and copairing transports; coalgebra and counit preservation by each cozipper; sliding of closed-window and handle operators; the Cardy reduction of an open handle through the closed sector; and cyclic rotation of an open product followed by a cozipper. In particular, define
$$
b_{ab}:=\epsilon_a\mu_{aba}:A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}\to k, \qquad d_{ab}:=\Delta_{aba}\eta_a:k\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{ba}.
$$
Both maps to algebraic duals induced by $b_{ab}$ and $b_{ba}$ are isomorphisms. With $b_C=\epsilon_C\mu_C$, $d_C=\Delta_C\eta_C$, $W_a=i_a^*i_a:C\to C$, $H=\mu_C\Delta_C:C\to C$, and $O_a=\mu_{aaa}\Delta_{aaa}:A_{aa}\to A_{aa}$, the typed consequences include
$$
\Delta_Ci_a^*=(i_a^*\otimes i_a^*)\Delta_{aaa},\qquad \epsilon_Ci_a^*=\epsilon_a,\qquad i_a^*O_a=W_ai_a^*.
$$
The same map identities hold in the formal symmetric monoidal presentation generated by the ten typed elementary surfaces and their equations in [[lem-elementary-surface-sewing-relations]]. Here the tensor unit replaces $k$, and finite-dimensional dual-isomorphism statements are confined to the vector-space specialization. Thus the identities may be used as surface rewrites before classification. This formal assertion is proved by faithful bending in step 1.5; equality of vector-space evaluations alone is not used to infer a surface equality.

derivations.claim: Bend every outgoing open interval into an incoming interval with reversed endpoint order, and every incoming closed circle into an outgoing circle, keeping the original slot markings and the explicit symmetry maps. The formal snakes give inverse unbending; geometrically these are the boundary-relative pairing/copy-pairing surfaces of [F3]–[F4]. It suffices to treat a connected surface with open source and closed target. By [F2] it has a finite expression in the ten generators. Delete its open units and counits by $\eta_a=i_a\eta_C$ and $\epsilon_a=\epsilon_Ci_a^*$. This deletes one open extremum at a time and creates none. Expand every packaged open window $O_{ab}^{s}=\mu_{asb}\Delta_{asb}$ when counting open coproducts. The resulting expression is a finite directed acyclic graph of typed wires and generator occurrences. Acyclicity follows from its expression by tensor and composition, not from any assertion about the undirected graph.

If open coproducts remain, choose one $\Delta_{abc}:A_{ac}\to A_{ab}\otimes A_{bc}$ with no open coproduct in its strict directed downstream graph. Such a choice exists because the graph is finite and acyclic. This is the consequence for which LP uses a minimum **downstream** height; the source's height convention is toward the target. Until its outputs encounter a cozipper, their open continuation wires cannot branch: the only vertex with multiple open outputs is an open coproduct, absent downstream by the choice. Each path therefore passes through a chain of open products, eventually reaching either the other path at a product, or a cozipper. There is no open exterior target, no remaining open counit, and no other generator accepting an open wire. In particular a zipper cannot be the next vertex on an open wire, since its domain is $C$.

Choose a first event consisting either of the first merge of these two open paths or of a cozipper reached by either path. More precisely take a minimal such event in any topological ordering of the finite downstream graph. Before this event, every additional input feeding the open-product paths is independent of the two distinguished coproduct outputs. If an additional input depended on one of them through an open path, that would already be a merge; if it depended on one through a closed path, that path would already have passed through a cozipper. Either possibility contradicts the first-event choice. Thus all intervening side inputs can be retained as independent typed input blocks, even if their upstream expressions share other suppliers or contain coproducts that are not downstream of the marked one. Indexed associativity flattens each path into its actual ordered word without changing that order. We can therefore isolate the marked coproduct and this first event as a subexpression with independent side-input blocks and with the rest of the original expression attached to its output ports. The three finite possibilities are an uncrossed merge, a crossed merge, or a cozipper event, with the two left/right cozipper positions distinct.

For an uncrossed merge the flattened product has the form $L p Y q R$, where $\Delta_{abc}(x)=\sum p_{ab}\otimes q_{bc}$ and $Y$ has type $A_{bb}$. The outer words $L,R$ remain in the context. Associativity isolates the sandwich $pYq$. For a crossed merge the flattened word has the form $L q Y p R$, where $Y$ has type $A_{ca}$; again isolate the middle sandwich. These are the two possible orders of the two distinguished wires in an ordered product. At a cozipper event the flattened input has the form $L p R$, or $L q R$. The cyclic cozipper identity moves the external block $L$ round the trace, yielding $pY$ or $Yq$, with $Y$ the indexed product of the remaining side inputs in its preserved cyclic order. Thus the four typed identities in the following steps exhaust the first-event configurations, including paths of arbitrary finite length.

The uncrossed sandwich has the formal identity $\sum pYq=\mu_{acc}(x,i_ci_b^*(Y)):A_{ac}\otimes A_{bb}\to A_{ac}.$ Here is its full derivation. Frobenius and the unit give $\Delta_{abc}=(\mu_{acb}\otimes1_{bc})(1_{ac}\otimes d_{cb})$, with $d_{cb}=\Delta_{cbc}\eta_c$. Write the copairing output wires as $r:A_{cb},q:A_{bc}$. Associativity changes $((xr)Y)q$ to $x((rY)q)$. The copairing symmetry is $d_{cb}=\tau_{bc,cb}d_{bc}$, and Frobenius gives $\Delta_{bcb}=(1_{bc}\otimes\mu_{cbb})(d_{bc}\otimes1_{bb})$. Consequently the formal composite with output string $\sum(rY)q$ is exactly $\mu_{cbc}\tau_{bc,cb}\Delta_{bcb}$, which is $i_ci_b^*$ by the colored Cardy equation. This proves the identity as an equality of composites. For a crossed sandwich, the first Frobenius identity with labels $(a,b,c,a)$ is $\Delta_{aba}\mu_{aca}=(1_{ab}\otimes\mu_{bca})(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{ca}).$ Compose with $\mu_{bab}\tau_{ab,ba}$. Colored Cardy then gives the separately typed identity $\sum qYp=i_bi_a^*\mu_{aca}(x,Y):A_{ac}\otimes A_{ca}\to A_{bb}.$ Both replacements remove the marked open coproduct and create no open coproduct at their completed endpoints. Reflected external positions are handled by tensoring these equalities with $L,R$ and composing with their ordered products. If the uncrossed side word is empty, take $Y=\eta_b$ in the derivation and simplify $i_b^*\eta_b=i_b^*i_b\eta_C=W_b\eta_C$; the endpoint is $\mu_{acc}(1_{ac}\otimes i_cW_b\eta_C)$ and has no open unit or coproduct. If the crossed side word is empty, its type $A_{ca}$ forces $a=c$; use $Y=\eta_a$ and the unit equation to obtain $i_bi_a^*x$, precisely Cardy. No open unit is retained in either result.

For a left cozipper event the exact subexpression, after the cyclic rotation of step 4.1, is $F_{abc}:=(i_a^*\mu_{aba}\otimes1_{bc})(1_{ab}\otimes\tau_{bc,ba})(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{ba}):A_{ac}\otimes A_{ba}\to C\otimes A_{bc}.$ Indexed cyclicity $i_a^*\mu_{aba}=i_b^*\mu_{bab}\tau_{ab,ba}$ and tensor naturality give $F_{abc}=(i_b^*\otimes1_{bc})(\mu_{bab}\otimes1_{bc})(1_{ba}\otimes\Delta_{abc})\tau_{ac,ba}.$ The second Frobenius identity with labels $(b,a,b,c)$ changes the middle two factors to $\Delta_{bbc}\mu_{bac}$. Finally the copairing transport yields $F_{abc}=(1_C\otimes\mu_{bbc})(1_C\otimes i_b\otimes1_{bc})(d_C\otimes1_{bc})\mu_{bac}\tau_{ac,ba}.$ For clarity the transport is formal: $\Delta_{bbc}=(1_{bb}\otimes\mu_{bbc})(d_{bb}\otimes1_{bc})$, and $(i_b^*\otimes1_{bb})d_{bb}=(1_C\otimes i_b)d_C$. Thus no open coproduct remains at the completed endpoint. The output types are still $C\otimes A_{bc}$, so any downstream continuation, including a later zipper or reconnection, is attached unchanged.

The right cozipper position has type $A_{ac}\otimes A_{cb}\to A_{ab}\otimes C$ and the composite $G_{abc}:=(1_{ab}\otimes i_c^*\mu_{cbc})(1_{ab}\otimes\tau_{bc,cb})(\Delta_{abc}\otimes1_{cb}).$ Cyclicity changes $i_c^*(Yq)$ to $i_b^*(qY)$. The first Frobenius identity with labels $(a,b,c,b)$ then gives $G_{abc}=(1_{ab}\otimes i_b^*)\Delta_{abb}\mu_{acb}$ $=(\mu_{abb}\otimes1_C)(1_{ab}\otimes i_b\otimes1_C)(1_{ab}\otimes d_C)\mu_{acb}.$ The last equality uses $\Delta_{abb}=(\mu_{abb}\otimes1_{bb})(1_{ab}\otimes d_{bb})$ and $(1_{bb}\otimes i_b^*)d_{bb}=(i_b\otimes1_C)d_C$. Empty side words give the corresponding direct cozipper transport after the unit is canceled. Every external interval type is retained; the change from cozipper basepoint $c$ to $b$ is precisely the stated cyclic identity.

Replace the first-event subexpression by the applicable first-event equality just proved, then repeat the selection of step 2.1. Each completed replacement deletes one actual open coproduct occurrence and creates none; arbitrary side-input and downstream blocks are attached by tensor and composition, so they are not duplicated. The finite number of actual open coproduct vertices is therefore a strictly decreasing outer measure. This terminates with no open coproduct. It also eliminates every packaged open window, because its coproduct was included in that count. Thus termination uses the primitive coproduct count and no simultaneous normalizing sweep.

In the resulting expression every connected subgraph consisting of open wires and open products is a finite product tree: products have one output, and no open coproduct can branch an open wire. Its leaves are exterior incoming intervals or zipper outputs; its root is a cozipper, because there is no exterior outgoing interval or open counit. Unary identity segments are ignored. A component with no product is one leaf feeding one cozipper. For each tree, associativity flattens its leaf products in their actual cyclic boundary order. If a zipper is its sole leaf, $i_a^*i_a=W_a$ removes it. Otherwise indexed centrality and associativity move a selected zipper leaf $i_s(c)$ successively through the adjacent open products to the basepoint of the cozipper. The precise centrality equality is $\mu_{aab}(i_a\otimes1_{ab})=\mu_{abb}(1_{ab}\otimes i_b)\tau_{C,A_{ab}}:C\otimes A_{ab}\to A_{ab}.$ Removing the zipper from a cyclic word leaves a correctly indexed cyclic word of the remaining leaves: its two neighboring free labels had been the same basepoint color. Thus it reduces to a terminal zipper/product/cozipper configuration with one remaining diagonal open input.

The terminal equality is $i_a^*\mu_{aaa}(i_a\otimes1_{aa})=\mu_C(1_C\otimes i_a^*):C\otimes A_{aa}\to C.$ To prove it formally, bend its target by $b_C$, retaining a full additional $C$ input. On $C\otimes C\otimes A_{aa}$, pairing adjunction, invariance, the zipper algebra equation, pairing adjunction again, and closed invariance give in order $b_C(1\otimes i_a^*\mu_{aaa}(i_a\otimes1))=b_a(i_a\otimes\mu_{aaa}(i_a\otimes1))=b_a(\mu_{aaa}(i_a\otimes i_a)\otimes1)$ $=b_a(i_a\mu_C\otimes1)=b_C(\mu_C\otimes i_a^*)=b_C(1\otimes\mu_C(1\otimes i_a^*)).$ Faithful unbending cancels the closed snake and proves the equality. Centrality gives the reflected input order $i_a^*\mu_{aaa}(1\otimes i_a)=\mu_C(i_a^*\otimes1)$. Each completed removal deletes one zipper and creates none; each preceding push crosses a finite number of products on its unique path to the cozipper. Repeating terminates by the number of zipper leaves. No open coproduct or extremum is created.

The surviving open trees have only exterior incoming interval leaves and one cozipper root. They are precisely the components of the boundary carrying the marked incoming intervals: a product disk concatenates successive interval slots along their common free-edge label, and the cozipper closes that ordered string into one boundary cycle. This follows directly from the generator boundary words in [F3], rather than from a proposed classification theorem. Each tree therefore has the form $T_j=i_{a_0}^*\mu_{a_0a_1\cdots a_q}^{(q)}$ with $a_q=a_0$, keeping its full marked slot and endpoint-color sequence. The cyclic cozipper identity equates all starting points of this same cycle. A cycle cannot be split or reconnected by any preceding replacement because every replacement is an actual boundary-relative equality. Restore their prescribed least-slot order by the explicit symmetry $P$ of [F5].

It remains to normalize a connected graph made entirely of closed Frobenius generators, the closed inputs from these $r$ open-cycle trees, windows $W_s$, and the $n$ exterior closed outputs. The following finite closed-spider fusion proves the purposes of LP stages VII–VIII directly. Write $S_{mn}=\Delta_C^{[n]}\mu_C^{[m]}$ for $m,n\ge0$. If one output of $S_{mn}$ is glued to one input of $S_{pq}$, where $n,p\ge1$ and $m,q\ge0$, then, after retaining the other ports in their marked order, the fusion equality is $(1_C^{\otimes(n-1)}\otimes S_{pq})(S_{mn}\otimes1_C^{\otimes(p-1)})=S_{m+p-1,n+q-1},$ with the tensor permutations placing the sewn ports last and first. For completeness this identity is valid in every orientation: bend all remaining ports to inputs. Define $t_k=\epsilon_C\mu_C^{[k]}:C^{\otimes k}\to k$, including $t_0=\epsilon_C\eta_C$. Associativity and commutativity make $t_k$ invariant under all input permutations. Pairing invariance identifies the bent form of every $S_{mn}$ with $t_{m+n}$. Contracting one input of $t_u$ with one of $t_v$ through $d_C$ gives $t_{u+v-2}$ for $u,v\ge1$: reassociate the uncontracted inputs into their two products; pairing invariance moves those products to the two free legs of the contracted $b_C$ pairings, and the snake contracts the middle $d_C$ to the single pairing of the two products. When one list is empty its product is $\eta_C$ and the same equality is the unit/counit equation. This supplies all induction base and empty cases, and proves fusion after faithful unbending. Thus it is a formal consequence of associativity, commutativity, Frobenius, unit/counit and the snakes, not an assumption about all surface morphisms.

There is also a self-gluing equality: joining any one input and output port of $S_{m+1,n+1}$ produces $\Delta_C^{[n]}H\mu_C^{[m]}$, where $H=\mu_C\Delta_C$. Indeed bend its remaining ports to inputs; the self-gluing inserts $d_C$ into two arguments of $t_{m+n+2}$. Commutativity and associativity put those two arguments next to each other; their product is $\mu_Cd_C=H\eta_C$. Frobenius gives $H\mu_C=\mu_C(H\otimes1)=\mu_C(1\otimes H)$, so the contracted map is $\epsilon_CH\mu_C^{[m+n]}$. Faithful unbending gives the displayed equality. Iterating a self-gluing inserts one further $H$ each time; no additional generators or unreduced cases are hidden in this formula.

Keep each colored window as a unary vertex and choose an undirected spanning tree of the finite connected closed graph, treating the marked input/output ports as external legs. A window slides through every closed product and coproduct by the typed window relations, so it can be carried along the chosen tree to a distinguished central strand while retaining its label. Its passage through a unit, counit or an edge with a bent orientation is the same formal relation after bending with a snake. Contract the spanning-tree edges between the Frobenius vertices by step 10.1; each contraction lowers the number of vertices by one and never identifies or permutes marked external slots. If needed insert an identity spider $S_{11}$ to give a vertex to a component consisting initially of a single strand. Every remaining internal edge now self-glues two ports of the one spider, so apply step 11.1 once per such edge. This algorithm terminates by the finite tree-edge count followed by the finite remaining-edge count. It gives $\Delta_C^{[n]}H^g W_{s_1}\cdots W_{s_w}\mu_C^{[r]}.$ The window operators commute because their formal closed-module slide identifies each with multiplication by its own state $W_s\eta_C$ in the commutative object $C$; the same argument slides them across $H$. Hence their order is immaterial, while each color and multiplicity is retained. This is the finite inversion-ordering purpose of LP IX without a repeated normalization sweep.

The exponent $g$ is the genus of the original component. After window vertices are suppressed, a connected graph with $v$ vertices and $e$ internal edges has $e-v+1$ non-tree edges. Fusing one tree seam between two genus-zero spiders makes one genus-zero spider, as its planar cut models show. Closing two of its circle ports leaves Euler characteristic unchanged and lowers the number of full boundary components by two, so it raises genus by one. Each window $W_s=i_s^*i_s$ is an annulus-with-window: its genus is zero, it contributes one free boundary circle of color $s$, and it changes Euler characteristic by minus one while leaving the graph's first Betti number unchanged as a unary insertion. Each open tree $T_j$ is genus zero and replaces one closed input circle by exactly one mixed open boundary cycle. Thus the surface built by the algorithm has exactly the original boundary partition and boundary cycles, the original free-window multiplicities, and genus $e-v+1=g$. These assertions also follow from the fact that every contraction was an actual boundary-relative equality. No colored arc is identified with a different color.

In the empty cases, $r=0$ means there is no exterior source after bending, and the initial closed spider product is precisely $\mu_C^{[0]}=\eta_C$; $n=0$ means there is no exterior target, and its final closed spider coproduct is precisely $\Delta_C^{[0]}=\epsilon_C$. These are already included in the fusion and self-gluing formulas, rather than inferred from an ill-typed assertion that a counit's own domain is empty. In particular a connected component with no black boundary is exactly $\epsilon_CH^gW_M\eta_C$. Combining the open-tree and closed-graph reductions, the resulting full composite is exactly the candidate word $N(M)$ in [F5]. Unbend the original marked slots using the inverse snakes of step 1.1.

Every finite transformation above is a formal consequence of the elementary boundary-relative equalities of [F3] and formally derived identities of [F4]; it therefore gives equality of actual surface morphisms. Hence $[M]=[N(M)]$. If two connected surfaces have the listed identical marked data, [F5] gives the same word for both, so they are equal. Conversely, an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism relative to all black parameterizations preserves each component, its genus, its colored free circles, and the cyclic orders and complete color sequences of the marked intervals. The same data are therefore necessary. For a disconnected surface apply the finite argument separately to each connected component, tensor the resulting words, and restore the original marked source and target orders by their symmetry cylinders. This proves both the full colored classification and the stated tensor formula, including components without marked black slots.
